docs.title: break-even
docs.text: Finds the break-even point for a product or business: the number of units you must sell so that revenue exactly covers fixed costs plus variable costs. It also shows break-even revenue and the contribution margin per unit. Launching a product or running a business without knowing the break-even point risks pricing that can never cover costs. The calculation separates what must be sold before profit exists, which anchors pricing, marketing, and budget decisions. Founders pricing a product, small-business owners planning costs, and anyone evaluating a new offering's viability. Decide if a selling price covers fixed and variable costs Set a sales target before a product becomes profitable See how a price change shifts the break-even point Estimate how fixed-cost cuts reduce required volume Evaluate whether a new product line is worth launching Budget marketing spend against the volume it must generate Enter total fixed costs for the period Enter variable cost per unit Enter the selling price per unit Read the units and revenue needed to break even Adjust price or costs to see how the point moves Use the contribution margin to reason about volume targets $50,000 fixed, $15 variable, $40 price → 2,000 units, $80,000 revenue $20,000 fixed, $8 variable, $20 price → 1,667 units, $33,333 revenue $50,000 fixed, $15 variable, $45 price → 1,667 units — a $5 price rise cuts required volume by 17% $30,000 fixed, $10 variable, $25 price → 2,000 units with a $15 contribution margin per unit Be honest about all fixed costs, from rent to software Update variable costs whenever suppliers or labor change Use break-even as a floor, not a target — profit needs more Re-run the math if the price changes Stress-test with a higher variable cost to build a safety margin Excluding fixed costs like rent, salaries, and tools Understating variable cost per unit Pricing below variable cost, making break-even impossible Treating break-even units as if profit comes automatically Forgetting that break-even assumes every unit sells at the same price Ignoring the cash-flow timing of when fixed costs actually come due Break-even units and revenue calculation Fixed costs, variable costs, and selling price inputs Contribution margin per unit Multi-currency support 100% browser-based and private SBA — Break-Even Analysis

docs.title: cagr-calculator
docs.text: Calculates the Compound Annual Growth Rate of an investment. Given a beginning value, an ending value, and the number of years, it returns the constant annual growth rate that would produce the final value. Simple return figures don't capture how long an investment grew. CAGR smooths that fluctuation into one annual rate, so different investments and holding periods can be compared apples-to-apples. Investors, portfolio managers, and analysts measuring fund or stock performance across multi-year periods. Normalize returns of investments held for different durations Compare mutual funds and stocks that have been held different lengths of time Report one growth rate for a whole holding period Decide between assets by their annualized growth rather than total gain Measure business revenue or profit growth over several years Benchmark a fund's return against an index like the S&P 500 Enter the value you started with (beginning value) Enter the current or final value Enter the number of years of the holding period Read the CAGR as an annual percentage Compare several investments using their CAGR figures Re-run with fees included for a net-of-cost rate $1,000 grows to $2,100 in 5 years → CAGR ≈ 16.0% $25,000 grows to $48,000 in 4 years → CAGR ≈ 17.7% $100 to $161 in 3 years → CAGR ≈ 17.2% $10,000 to $13,000 in 4 years → CAGR ≈ 6.8%, even though the total gain was 30% Use CAGR for comparisons, not as a prediction of the future Include all fees exactly as they affect the value Compare only investments with the same timeframes Use the net-of-cost end value for accuracy Remember CAGR flattens volatility — two funds with the same CAGR can have very different risk Treating a single year's gain as a multi-year rate Forgetting to include brokerage fees and dividends in beginning/end values Comparing CAGRs of periods of very different length Entering the rate as a fraction of a whole year Using CAGR to forecast — it describes past growth, not future returns Annualized growth rate Begin and end value inputs Multi-year, compounding-aware math Simple cross-investment comparisons 100% browser-based and private Investor.gov — Compound Annual Growth Rate

docs.title: capital-gains-tax
docs.text: Estimates capital gains tax for India, the US, the UK, Canada, and Australia. It computes your gain (sale price − purchase price − expenses), applies each country's holding-period rules, exemptions, and rates — including short-term vs long-term treatment, the Indian LTCG exemption, UK Annual Exempt Amount, Canadian 50% inclusion, and the Australian CGT discount. Capital gains tax works completely differently across countries: some distinguish short- vs long-term, some apply flat rates, some use discounts or inclusion rates. A country-aware calculator applies the correct rules automatically instead of guessing a single rate. Investors selling shares or crypto, homeowners selling property abroad or at home, expats planning cross-border sales, and anyone comparing how different countries would tax the same disposal. Estimate tax before selling listed shares held long-term in India (₹1.25L exemption check) Compare short-term vs long-term tax on a US stock sale, including NIIT Work out UK CGT after the £3,000 annual exempt amount at basic or higher rates See how Canada's 50% inclusion rate combines with your province's marginal rate Check whether the Australian 50% discount applies after 12 months of holding Plan whether to sell this year or next based on exemption resets and holding thresholds Select your country — currency switches automatically but can be overridden Choose the asset type: listed shares, unlisted shares, property, crypto, or other Enter how long you held the asset where the country uses holding periods Enter the purchase price, sale price, and eligible expenses Add country-specific inputs when shown (filing status, taxable income, province, residency) Read the gain, taxable amount, estimated tax, and per-item breakdown India: listed shares bought ₹100,000, sold ₹300,000 after 18 months → gain ₹200,000; ₹1.25L exempt; 12.5% on ₹75,000 → ₹9,375 US: $10,000 long-term gain with $40,000 taxable income → part taxed at 0%, remainder at 15% UK: £20,000 gain with £30,000 income → £3,000 AEA applied; £7,700 at 18% + rest at 24% Canada: $40,000 gain in Ontario → 50% inclusion adds $20,000 to income at combined marginal rates Australia: $40,000 gain held 24 months by a resident → 50% discount halves the taxable gain Include every eligible cost — brokerage, stamp duty, legal fees — they reduce the taxable gain Check the exact acquisition date against the holding threshold before selling For income-dependent systems (US, UK, CA, AU), enter realistic other income for an accurate marginal rate Use the correct asset type — India taxes crypto at a flat 30% regardless of holding period Treat results as estimates; confirm with a qualified tax professional Applying one universal 12-month rule everywhere — India uses 12/24 months by asset type and the UK/Canada use none at all Forgetting that India's indexation benefit ended for transfers on or after 23 July 2024 Assuming crypto is treated like shares in India — VDAs are taxed at a flat 30% and losses cannot be offset Ignoring NIIT (US) or Medicare levy (Australia) which add to the headline rate Entering gross income instead of taxable income in systems that need your marginal band Multi-country support (India, US, UK, Canada, Australia) Multi-currency support with auto-switching Asset type selection (shares, property, crypto, other) Holding period rules per country Country-specific inputs (filing status, province, residency) Per-item tax breakdown 100% browser-based and private Income Tax India — Capital Gains IRS — Topic 409: Capital Gains and Losses GOV.UK — Capital Gains Tax rates and allowances Canada Revenue Agency — Capital gains ATO — Capital gains tax

Different programming languages enforce different naming conventions (camelCase for JS, snake_case for Python, kebab-case for CSS). Developers need to convert between conventions quickly when moving between projects or refactoring codebases without manual search-and-replace operations. Full-stack developers working across multiple languages, API designers normalizing field names, database administrators mapping between conventions, and anyone refactoring large codebases with inconsistent naming. docs.title: chmod-calculator
docs.text: Calculates Unix file permission modes with a visual checkbox grid. Toggle Read, Write, and Execute permissions for Owner, Group, and Others and see the octal (e.g., 755), symbolic (e.g., rwxr-xr-x), and chmod command output update in real time. Includes common presets and one-click copy for all output formats. Unix file permissions can be confusing — converting between octal numbers, symbolic notation, and actual permissions requires mental arithmetic that is easy to get wrong. This tool provides a visual, error-free way to configure and understand file permissions. System administrators managing file permissions on Linux/Unix servers, developers setting up project file permissions, DevOps engineers configuring deployment scripts, and students learning about Unix security. Calculate the chmod value for a desired permission set without doing mental math Convert between octal notation (755) and symbolic notation (rwxr-xr-x) Quickly apply common permission presets like 755 for executables or 644 for config files Generate the exact chmod command to copy and paste into a terminal Learn how Unix permission bits map to octal values using the visual grid Toggle the checkboxes for each permission (Read/Write/Execute) for Owner, Group, and Others Watch the octal, symbolic, and command outputs update automatically Or type a 3-digit octal number directly into the input field and press Apply Use the preset buttons for common permission sets like 755 or 644 Click on any output box to copy that value to your clipboard Owner: rwx, Group: r-x, Others: r-x -> Octal: 755 -> Symbolic: rwxr-xr-x Owner: rw-, Group: r--, Others: r-- -> Octal: 644 -> Symbolic: rw-r--r-- Use 644 for regular files that should be readable by all but writable only by the owner Use 755 for directories and executable scripts that all users should be able to enter/execute Use 700 or 600 for sensitive files that only the owner should access Avoid using 777 unless you fully understand the security implications Always double-check permissions before applying them to production systems Setting 777 on files as a quick fix — this gives everyone full read/write/execute access Confusing the order: it is Owner, Group, Others — not Others, Group, Owner Forgetting that execute permission on a directory allows listing its contents Using 666 for files that need to be executable — add the execute bit (766 or 755) Convert between numeric and symbolic modes Visual checkbox grid for permissions Copy the chmod command chmod(1) — man page

docs.title: chronometer

docs.title: code-complexity
docs.text: Analyzes JavaScript and TypeScript code in the browser to estimate cyclomatic complexity, lines of code (total, code, comment, and blank), and a simple maintainability indicator. Highlights which functions are the most complex so you know where to refactor. Complex code is harder to test and maintain, and it correlates with bugs, but it's hard to judge by eye. A quick complexity metric lets developers flag the riskiest functions and protect code quality before complexity becomes unmanageable. Developers and tech leads performing code reviews, maintainers measuring technical and cognitive debt, and engineers deciding where to split or refactor functions. Measure cyclomatic complexity of a module before a review Find the functions with the highest complexity to target refactoring Track complexity changes between refactors of a file Get an at-a-glance maintainability score for a code snippet Benchmark a legacy file before deciding whether to refactor or rewrite it Paste your JavaScript or TypeScript code into the editor The analyzer reads LOC counts and complexity automatically Review the overall score for the snippet Read the function-level breakdown to find the highest-complexity functions Use the recommendations to plan your refactoring Run it again after refactoring to confirm complexity dropped A function with 5 if/else branches and 2 loops → cyclomatic complexity ~8 A 20-line pure function with no branches → cyclomatic complexity 1 A module with many >10-complexity functions → the module is likely hard to maintain LOC breakdown: 120 total, 95 code, 12 comments, 13 blank Keep per-function complexity under roughly 10 to make each function easy to test Use the metric as a signal for refactoring, not a hard law Re-check complexity after each refactor to confirm it lowered Combine complexity with readability and test coverage for a full picture Investigate complexity outliers in code review before merging Treating high complexity as the only indicator of poor quality Gaming the metric by splitting functions artificially Ignoring nested conditionals that inflate perceived readability Comparing complexity across unrelated languages or paradigms Measuring a single file while ignoring how it couples with the rest of the module Cyclomatic complexity per function Total LOC, code, comment, and blank counts Maintainability indicator Highest-complexity function highlight Works with JavaScript and TypeScript 100% browser-based and private Cyclomatic Complexity — McCabe (IEEE)

docs.title: color-converter
docs.text: Converts colors between six formats (HEX, RGB, RGBA, HSL, HSLA, HSV, CMYK) with automatic format detection on paste. Features a palette generator for shades, tints, complementary, triadic, and tetradic schemes, and calculates Delta E (CIE76) color difference for precise color comparison. Color management is critical in web design and UI development. Developers frequently need to convert between color models, check accessibility compliance, and generate harmonious color schemes — tasks that previously required multiple specialized tools or manual calculations. Frontend developers and UI designers implementing design systems, accessibility engineers auditing color contrast, digital artists working across color spaces, and branding specialists creating consistent palettes. docs.title: compound-interest-calculator
docs.text: Projects how a lump sum plus regular monthly contributions grows over time with compound interest. Shows the matured value, the total amount contributed, and the interest earned on top, so you can see exactly how much of the final balance is your own money versus growth. Compound interest is the engine behind long-term saving, but the numbers are easy to underestimate. A calculator turns the compound growth formula into an instant projection so investors can see what small monthly amounts become over decades. Long-term savers, retirement planners, students learning about investing, financial advisors, and anyone comparing lump-sum deposits against systematic monthly investing. Project how much a fixed deposit or index fund grows with monthly additions Compare lump-sum investing vs. equal monthly contributions over the same horizon Estimate the future value of a retirement fund decades from now See how interest earned exceeds contributions over long horizons Model an education or down-payment savings goal with monthly top-ups Demonstrate to younger savers why starting early beats investing more later Enter your starting amount in Initial amount Add a monthly contribution to model ongoing savings, or set it to 0 for a pure lump sum Set the expected annual interest rate in percent Choose the number of years you will let it grow Read the matured value, total contributed, and interest earned Adjust any input and watch the projection update so you can test scenarios $10,000 initial, $500/month at 7% for 10 years → ~$107,000 matured $0 initial, $200/month at 8% for 30 years → ~$298,000 matured $50,000 initial, $0/month at 5% for 20 years → ~$135,600 matured $10,000 initial, $500/month at 7% for 30 years → ~$150,000 contributed but ~$650,000+ matured thanks to compounding Use a conservative rate estimate and review it periodically as markets change Recall that the projection is pre-tax and pre-inflation — real returns will be lower Increase your contribution when income grows; docs.title: credit-card-payoff
docs.text: Simulates paying off a credit card balance with a fixed monthly payment. It applies the card's monthly interest and shows the payoff time, total interest, and total paid, so you can compare how different monthly payments change the finish line. A card balance grows because monthly interest can outpace the minimum payment. Seeing exactly how many months a fixed payment will take — and how much interest accumulates — helps people choose a realistic payment that actually reduces the balance. Anyone carrying a credit card balance who wants to know how long it takes to clear at their current payment, or how much faster extra payments finish the job. See how long the balance takes at the current payment Compare payments to find an affordable acceleration Understand how much interest the balance will cost Set a payoff milestone for a specific card Decide whether a balance-transfer offer is worth the fee Check whether a modest extra payment meaningfully shortens the payoff Enter the current card balance Enter the card's annual APR Enter your fixed monthly payment Read the payoff months, total interest, and total paid Raise the monthly payment to see how much sooner you finish Compare two payment amounts side by side to pick a plan $5,000 at 19.99% APR, $200/month → about 31 months, ~$1,196 interest $2,000 at 24% APR, $100/month → about 25 months, ~$455 interest $5,000 at 19.99% APR, $250/month → about 24 months and ~$900 interest — an extra $50/month saves ~$300 $3,000 at 22% APR, $85/month → interest alone exceeds the payment, so the balance never falls Pay more than the monthly interest so the balance actually falls Stop adding new purchases while paying down Consider balance-transfer offers with care about fees Round the payment up to shave both months and interest Automate the payment so the plan actually happens Paying only the minimum — the payoff can stretch for decades Using a payment at or below the monthly interest (never finishes) Ignoring that new purchases add to the balance Assuming the APR applies once a year instead of monthly Choosing a huge payment that's not sustainable, then stopping CFPB — Credit Card Repayment

docs.title: cron-expression
docs.text: A visual cron expression builder that constructs cron schedules from human-friendly controls and displays the expression in real-time. Includes preset buttons (@yearly, @monthly, @weekly, @daily, @hourly), a human-readable description, a table showing the next 10 execution times, timezone selection, 6-field cron support (with seconds), @macro expansion, favorites/saved expressions, and export as systemd timer or crontab format. Cron expressions are notoriously error-prone to write by hand — a misplaced asterisk can cause a job to run too frequently or never. A visual builder eliminates syntax errors, provides immediate feedback through descriptions and execution preview, and supports multiple cron variants for the full spectrum of scheduling needs. DevOps engineers managing scheduled jobs, backend developers setting up cron tasks, system administrators automating maintenance scripts, and anyone learning cron syntax. But '*/1 * * * *' runs every minute, often unintended Forgetting cron uses server-local time — scheduling for 14:00 may not be 2 PM in your timezone Using @daily (0 0 * * *) when meaning @midnight — they are the same, but expectations may differ Copying systemd format into crontab — syntax differs; use correct export format for your target system Visual cron builder with every field explained Presets and @-macro shortcuts Preview the next scheduled runs Timezone-aware scheduling cron(8) — man page Blog: Cron Expression Generator

docs.title: csp-generator
docs.text: A visual Content Security Policy builder that generates CSP headers through an interactive directive editor. Features include a nonce generator for inline scripts/styles, presets for common environments (Strict CSP, WordPress, React/SPA), toggling between meta tag and HTTP header output formats, report-uri/report-to configuration, directives search/filter, and download of the final policy as a text file. CSP is one of the most effective defenses against XSS, but writing a correct policy manually is complex and error-prone. A visual builder helps developers craft policies that are both secure and functional by guiding them through each directive with clear descriptions. Security engineers configuring web application defenses, full-stack developers deploying CSP, DevOps engineers adding security headers, and compliance teams documenting security controls. Generate a strict CSP for a React SPA that uses inline scripts and styles Create a WordPress-compatible CSP allowing necessary inline scripts while blocking XSS Build a CSP with report-uri configured to send violation reports to a monitoring endpoint Generate both meta tag and HTTP header versions of the same policy Add nonce-based policy for a specific page with fresh nonces per request Audit an existing CSP by pasting it in, editing visually, and downloading the updated version Start with a preset (Strict, WordPress, React/SPA) or from scratch — directive editor lists all standard CSP directives Add/remove directives using toggles — each has a description explaining what sources it controls For each directive, specify allowed sources with autocomplete suggestions (self, domains, nonces, hashes, unsafe-inline, etc.) Use nonce generator for cryptographically random nonces for inline script and style tags Toggle between 'Meta Tag' and 'HTTP Header' — meta tags don't support frame-ancestors, sandbox, or report-to Configure reporting with report-uri URL and optional report-to endpoint name Download the completed policy as .txt or copy to clipboard — includes human-readable summary Preset: React/SPA | Customize: Add GA => Output: "default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' https://www.googletagmanager.com 'nonce-abc123'; style-src 'self' 'nonce-abc123'; img-src 'self' https://www.google-analytics.com" Preset: Strict CSP | Meta Tag => Output: '<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="base-uri 'self'; default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'nonce-{NONCE}' 'strict-dynamic'">' Start with Strict CSP preset and loosen only what breaks — principle of least privilege Use nonces rather than 'unsafe-inline' — same functionality without disabling XSS protection Always configure report-uri in production — violation reports help identify breaks before users notice Test in staging with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only before deploying to production Use HTTP header format when possible — more secure as it applies before page parsing begins Including 'unsafe-inline' alongside nonces — ignored when nonce is present but causes confusion Forgetting to regenerate nonces per request — static nonces defeat the purpose Adding excessive domain allowlists instead of using 'strict-dynamic' — creates maintenance burden Using meta tag for HTTP-header-only directives (frame-ancestors, sandbox, report-to) Setting default-src too permissively — it serves as fallback for all unlisted directives Visually build Content-Security-Policy headers Directive presets and per-source controls Live policy preview Copy the finished header Content Security Policy — W3C MDN — CSP

docs.title: csv-to-json
docs.text:
Converts CSV data to JSON with automatic delimiter detection (comma, tab, semicolon, pipe). Supports four JSON output formats: array of objects, array of arrays, column-oriented (object of arrays), and pretty-printed. Features configurable quote character handling, drag-and-drop file upload, a preview table showing the first 5 rows, and size comparison between CSV input and JSON output. CSV is the most common data exchange format from spreadsheets, databases, and analytics tools, but most APIs consume JSON. A reliable, format-flexible converter that handles embedded commas, custom delimiters, and large files saves developers from writing one-off parsing scripts. Data engineers transforming CSV exports, backend developers ingesting spreadsheet data into APIs, data scientists converting survey results, and anyone migrating from legacy CSV to modern JSON APIs. Convert an Excel-exported CSV of customer data to array-of-objects JSON for a REST API Transform a tab-separated TSV from a database export to JSON for a web dashboard Convert semicolon-separated CSV (common in European locales) to column-oriented JSON Preview first 5 rows of a large CSV to verify column mapping before full conversion Convert pipe-delimited CSV from a mainframe export to pretty-printed JSON Parse CSV with quoted fields containing embedded commas and newlines Paste CSV text or drag-and-drop a .csv file — delimiter is auto-detected and displayed Review 'Preview' table showing first 5 rows — verify columns/data types before full conversion Select JSON output format: 'Array of Objects', 'Array of Arrays', 'Column-Oriented', or 'Pretty-Printed' Configure options: quote character (double/single), header row (first row as keys or key0,key1...), encoding Click 'Convert' — JSON output appears with size comparison (CSV vs JSON byte count) Copy JSON or download as .json — use streaming mode for large datasets to avoid memory limits Input CSV: 'name,age,city
Alice,30,NYC
Bob,25,LA' | Array of Objects => '[{"name":"Alice","age":"30","city":"NYC"},{"name":"Bob","age":"25","city":"LA"}]' Input: 'product	price	stock
Widget	9.99	42' | Tab delimiter | Column-Oriented => '{"product":["Widget"],"price":["9.99"],"stock":["42"]}' Input CSV with quoted commas: 'name,note
Alice,"likes cats, dogs"' => '[{"name":"Alice","note":"likes cats, dogs"}]' Input without headers: '1,apple
2,banana' with headers off => '[{"key0":"1","key1":"apple"},{"key0":"2","key1":"banana"}]' Always check preview before converting — catches delimiter detection errors Use 'Array of Objects' for REST APIs; 'Column-Oriented' for large datasets where only some columns are needed Check for BOM in Excel-exported CSVs — tool handles BOM but verify first column name For very large files (>100 MB), use streaming or split into smaller chunks Specify correct quote character — wrong setting causes incorrect parsing of quoted fields Assuming auto-detected delimiter is always correct for short files Using 'Array of Arrays' when CSV has headers — headers become first data row Forgetting all CSV values are strings in JSON — no auto type coercion Parsing CSVs with inconsistent quote characters — pre-normalize first Converting CSV with empty trailing rows — produces null JSON entries; trim first Convert CSV to structured JSON Automatic delimiter detection Header row and type inference options Copy and download the JSON output RFC 4180 — CSV

docs.title: currency-converter
docs.text: Converts an amount from one currency to another using live exchange rates for 160+ world currencies. Rates are fetched from a public exchange-rate API and cached for 10 minutes. Shows the converted amount, the exchange rate applied, and a clearly visible rate timestamp so you always know how current the number is. Exchange rates move constantly and using a stale or wrong rate can misprice an invoice, budget, or travel plan. This tool gives a current, clearly dated rate in one click, plus context on how the mid-market rate differs from what banks charge. Freelancers and contractors invoicing across currencies, travelers budgeting abroad, online shoppers price-comparing, importers quoting in foreign currency, and anyone handling foreign currency transactions. Convert an invoice amount into your home currency before sending a quote Check what a foreign price actually equals in your currency before paying Estimate travel spending and build a daily budget for a trip Compare international prices when shopping online across marketplaces Verify a rate quoted by a bank or payment gateway against the live mid-market rate Convert project budgets between the currencies your clients pay in Enter the amount you want to convert Choose the source currency (From) — the currency the amount is in Choose the target currency (To) — the currency you want the result in Read the converted amount and the exchange rate used, along with its timestamp Press Refresh rates to load a fresh rate after 10 minutes Swap the From and To currencies with the swap button to check the reverse rate 100 USD to EUR at 1.0834 → €92.30 10,000 INR to USD at 74.5 → about $134.23 500 GBP to USD at 1.27 → about $635 1,000 JPY to EUR at 161.2 → about €6.20 Use a recent rate for accurate quotes, since rates change constantly Keep in mind banks and card networks add a margin over the mid-market rate — often 1-3% Refresh the rates once more right before a real transaction Confirm the target currency code for the country you need (e.g., EUR vs. GBP) For large transfers, compare the tool's rate with what your bank actually quotes Using a stale rate from memory or an old page Confusing the From and To direction, which inverts the conversion Assuming the rate shown is the final rate after bank fees and margins Mixing currency codes (USD vs US dollar abbreviations) or using the wrong country's currency Forgetting that weekend rates are often frozen and Monday markets can gap open.er-api.com — Live Exchange Rates

docs.title: date-calculator
docs.text: Performs date arithmetic and computes the exact duration between two dates. Add or subtract days, weeks, months, or years from a start date, and view the resulting date plus a day-of-week calendar preview. Also calculates the precise difference (years, months, days, hours, minutes) between any two dates. Date math is deceptively tricky — months and years have uneven lengths, and adding 'one month' can land on an invalid day. A dedicated calculator removes the ambiguity and produces correct calendar arithmetic every time. Project managers planning milestones, developers computing deadlines and durations, HR teams handling leave and tenure, and anyone tracking event or payment schedules. docs.title: date-formatter
docs.text: Formats a date and time into more than 20 common patterns, including ISO 8601, RFC 2822, Unix timestamps (seconds and milliseconds), US locale strings, and ordered year-month-day variants. A formatter that shows exactly what a given timestamp looks like in different notations and timezones saves time when debugging data pipelines. Back-end and API developers working with timestamps, data engineers transforming records, QA engineers verifying date handling, and anyone adapting dates between systems. See how a Unix timestamp renders as an ISO 8601 or RFC 2822 string Verify the correct format to send to a third-party API Convert between local time and UTC for log correlation Produce a consistent date string for a database or report Pick an input date, either from the picker or by entering a Unix timestamp Select the timezone to interpret the value in Since the pattern list updates automatically, choose your preferred output format Copy the formatted result for use in your code or document Switch between milliseconds and seconds for Unix-style timestamps Input 1783800000000 ms → ISO 8601: 2026-07-11T06:40:00.000Z (UTC) Input 2026-08-07 14:00 → RFC 2822: Fri, 07 Aug 2026 14:00:00 +0000 Input 1750000000 s → Locale (US): July 1, 2025 at 12:00 AM Input 2026-01-15 08:30 → YMD: 20260115 0830 Always confirm whether a timestamp is seconds or milliseconds (10 vs 13 digits) Serialize dates in ISO 8601 UTC when storing or exchanging them Specify a timezone explicitly instead of relying on server default Use RFC 2822 for email and legacy HTTP headers Treating a millisecond timestamp as seconds and dividing incorrectly Assuming the server and browser timezones are the same Using year-first vs day-first formats inconsistently across systems Ignoring the offset marker when parsing ISO strings that lack 'Z' Copying a formatted string without recording the timezone it was produced in 20+ date and time output patterns ISO 8601, RFC 2822, Unix, and locale formats Seconds and milliseconds timestamp support Timezone selection One-click copy of results 100% browser-based and private ISO 8601 — Date and Time Format RFC 3339 — Date and Time on the Internet

docs.title: debt-payoff
docs.text: Builds a debt payoff plan from your debts, minimum payments, and a monthly budget. You can choose the snowball or avalanche strategy to see the payoff order, total months, and total interest paid, and compare which strategy finishes faster. Carrying multiple debts is overwhelming, and paying minimums across every card can extend payoff for years. A simple plan that directs every extra dollar at one clear target debt shortens the timeline and shows real progress with the snowball or avalanche order. Anyone with multiple credit cards, personal loans, student loans, or auto loans who wants a clear payoff sequence and knows what they can pay monthly. Order debts by smallest balance (snowball) for quick wins Order by highest APR (avalanche) to minimize interest See how an extra monthly budget shortens the plan Plan which card receives the surplus each month Compare snowball vs. avalanche to choose the strategy that fits your motivation Forecast when you will be debt-free and the total interest you'll pay Add each debt with its name, balance, APR, and minimum payment Set your total monthly budget for debt repayment Choose a strategy: snowball or avalanche Read the payoff months, total interest, and the payoff order Switch strategies to compare timelines and interest Increase the budget to see how much faster you finish Debt A $4,000 at 18.99% and Debt B $8,000 at 7.5%, $500/month → avalanche targets A first and saves the most interest Three small debts with $600/month using snowball → smallest balance cleared in the first months for momentum Two cards at 24% and 12% with a $300 budget → putting the extra $200 on the 24% card finishes faster and cheaper Set the budget at least equal to the sum of the minimum payments Keep paying minimums on every debt so nothing falls behind Understand snowball is motivational, avalanche is interest-optimal Re-run the plan if balances or minimums change Automate the payment to the target debt so the plan actually happens Setting a budget below the total minimums (no plan is possible) Entering an APR instead of a monthly rate by mistake Forgetting zero-APR promotional balances still count Assuming the payoff ignores interest charged during the plan Switching strategies mid-plan and losing the momentum of early wins CFPB — What is the Snowball Method of Paying Off Debt? docs.title: debt-to-income
docs.text: Calculates your debt-to-income (DTI) ratio: your total monthly debt payments divided by your gross monthly income, expressed as a percentage. docs.title: dns-lookup
docs.text: Performs DNS lookups across 11 record types (A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS, TXT, SOA, SRV, PTR, CAA, ANY). docs.title: down-payment-planner
docs.text: Plans how long it takes to save a home down payment based on your goal, current savings, monthly contribution, and the interest your savings earn. Shows the time to goal, the final balance, and the interest earned along the way. A down payment is often the biggest savings goal a household sets, and the timeline depends on far more than the goal itself. Knowing the time to goal — and the monthly amount required — turns an abstract target into a concrete plan. docs.title: encrypt-decrypt
docs.text: Encrypts and decrypts text using symmetric algorithms: AES, TripleDES, Rabbit, and RC4. Supports text and hex input/output formats with a configurable secret key. Output: hex string of the XOR-processed bytes. Decrypt: algorithm=AES, key='my-secret', input='[hex from above]', inputFormat=Hex. Output: 'Hello World' Use at least 16 characters for the secret key to resist brute-force attacks AES is the industry standard — prefer it over RC4 or Rabbit for real applications Always use authenticated encryption (AEAD) in production; this tool uses simplified XOR-based processing for learning Test with known plaintext/ciphertext pairs to verify algorithm behavior Using different keys for encryption and decryption, which produces garbled output Expecting production-grade security — this tool uses simplified cipher implementations for educational purposes Confusing hex output with text output when pasting ciphertext for decryption Using very short keys (< 8 chars) which provide insufficient key entropy Encrypt text with AES, TripleDES, Rabbit, and RC4 Passphrase-based key derivation Copy ciphertext or plaintext instantly Detect and decrypt supported ciphertexts NIST AES — FIPS 197
